group.title: Money and shopping
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A plastic card that takes money straight from your bank account when you pay.
examples: I paid for the groceries with my {debit card}.
wrong: I used my debit card, so the money came out of nobody’s account.

words.meaning: A machine in a wall where you can take out money from your bank account.
examples: I need to find a {cash machine} before the market.
wrong: I put coins into the cash machine to buy a cola.

words.meaning: A piece of paper money.
examples: She paid with a twenty-dollar {banknote}.
wrong: The banknote was a small round piece of metal.

words.meaning: Money you have kept and not spent, often in a bank.
examples: We used our {savings} to buy a car.
wrong: He had no savings because he had put lots of money aside.

words.meaning: To put money into a bank account.
examples: I {deposited} my paycheck this morning.
wrong: I deposited fifty dollars, so my account has fifty dollars less.

words.meaning: To take money out of a bank account.
examples: She {withdrew} two hundred dollars for the trip.
wrong: I withdrew some money by adding it to my account.

words.meaning: Extra money a bank pays you for saving, or that you pay for borrowing.
examples: My savings account pays two percent {interest}.
wrong: The bank pays interest by taking money out of your savings.

words.meaning: Money that you borrow and must pay back later.
examples: They took out a {loan} to buy a house.
wrong: A loan is money you never have to pay back.

words.meaning: A small label on a product that shows how much it costs.
examples: Check the {price tag} before you buy it.
wrong: The price tag told me what the shirt was made of, not the cost.

words.meaning: Being sold at a lower price than usual.
examples: These boots were {on sale}, so I saved thirty dollars.
wrong: The jacket was on sale, so it cost more than ever.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to take money from customers in a shop or bank.
examples: The {cashier} gave me my change and a receipt.
wrong: The cashier cooked our meal in the kitchen.

words.meaning: To give back something you bought and get a different one.
examples: Can I {exchange} these shoes for a bigger size?
wrong: I exchanged the shirt, so I kept the same one.

words.meaning: A written promise that a company will repair or replace a product if it breaks.
examples: The laptop has a two-year {warranty}.
wrong: The warranty says they will never fix it if it breaks.

words.meaning: To buy something, often something large or important.
examples: You can {purchase} tickets online.
wrong: I purchased the car by selling it to my neighbor.

words.meaning: To look at things in a shop without planning to buy anything.
examples: I like to {browse} in bookshops on Sundays.
wrong: I browsed the store by buying the first thing I saw and leaving.

words.meaning: Extra money you give to a waiter or driver to thank them.
examples: We left a good {tip} because the service was great.
wrong: We left a tip because the waiter was rude and slow.

words.meaning: Money you pay to do something or for a professional service.
examples: The museum’s entry {fee} is ten dollars.
wrong: There is no fee, so it costs fifteen dollars.

words.meaning: To ask someone to pay more than the correct price.
examples: The taxi driver {overcharged} us by twenty dollars.
wrong: The shop overcharged me, so I paid less than the real price.

words.meaning: To keep money over time so you can buy something later.
examples: He’s {saving up} for a new bike.
wrong: She saved up for a car by spending all her money each week.

words.meaning: Good quality for the price you pay.
examples: The meal was cheap and large, real {value for money}.
wrong: It’s great value for money: it costs a lot and breaks in a day.

words.meaning: Something that costs far more than it should.
examples: Ten dollars for a coffee? What a {rip-off}!
wrong: The meal was a rip-off because it was so cheap and good.

words.meaning: To argue with a seller to get a lower price.
examples: At the market you can {haggle} over the price of a rug.
wrong: I haggled with the seller and agreed to pay more than he asked.

words.meaning: The amount of money in a bank account.
examples: I checked my {balance} before buying the tickets.
wrong: My balance is the name of my bank.

words.meaning: Moving money from one bank account to another.
examples: I paid the rent by {bank transfer}.
wrong: I made a bank transfer by handing him some coins.

words.meaning: Owned and used by someone before you.
examples: I bought a {second-hand} bike for fifty dollars.
wrong: The phone was second-hand, so nobody had ever used it.

words.meaning: Completely new and never used.
examples: She drove home in a {brand-new} car.
wrong: My brand-new coat had holes from years of wear.

words.meaning: Costing quite a lot of money.
examples: That restaurant is nice but a bit {pricey}.
wrong: The hotel was pricey, so we paid almost nothing.

words.meaning: Costing more than it is really worth.
examples: The drinks at the stadium are {overpriced}.
wrong: The shirt was overpriced, so it was a great bargain.

words.meaning: A card a shop gives regular customers so they collect points and get discounts.
examples: Show your {loyalty card} to get points.
wrong: A loyalty card is for people who have never shopped there.

words.meaning: A printed paper or code you can use instead of money, or to get a lower price.
examples: I got a fifty-dollar {voucher} for my birthday.
wrong: I paid extra money because I had a voucher.

words.meaning: A small ticket that lets you pay less for something.
examples: Use this {coupon} to get ten percent off.
wrong: The coupon made my shopping cost much more.

words.meaning: Available in a shop to buy now.
examples: The shoes are {in stock} in all sizes.
wrong: That size is in stock, so the shop can’t sell it to you.

words.meaning: Having no more left to sell because everything has been bought.
examples: The concert was {sold out} in an hour.
wrong: The tickets were sold out, so there were plenty left.

words.meaning: To share the cost of a meal so each person pays part.
examples: There were four of us, so we {split the bill}.
wrong: We split the bill, so my friend paid for everything alone.

words.meaning: To spend a lot of money on something special.
examples: We {splashed out} on a fancy dinner for her birthday.
wrong: We splashed out by buying the cheapest thing on the menu.

words.meaning: To be very expensive.
examples: Fixing the roof {cost a fortune}.
wrong: The pen cost a fortune, only ten cents.

words.meaning: One of several regular payments you make for something.
examples: I’m paying for the sofa in monthly {installments}.
wrong: I paid in installments: the whole price at once.

words.meaning: A list from your bank that shows money paid in and out of your account.
examples: My {bank statement} shows every payment I made last month.
wrong: My bank statement was a letter about the weather.

words.meaning: To compare prices in different shops before buying.
examples: It pays to {shop around} before buying a new phone.
wrong: I shopped around by buying from the first store I saw.

words.meaning: Looking at things in shop windows without buying anything.
examples: We went {window-shopping} on the main street.
wrong: We went window-shopping and came home with ten bags of new clothes.
